The Wall — every chart Plotly can make

Grouped by the question you walked in holding, not by the chart's name. Find your question, then find the card whose data shape matches the columns you actually have. The chart's name is the last thing you need to know.

Every figure on this page is drawn from made-up numbers generated with numpy. Nothing here touched a database or the network. Press Ctrl-F and type a chart name to jump to it.

139 charts rendered 49 of 49 trace types used 6 listed but unrenderable here plotly 6.9.0 missing: scipy, statsmodels, kaleido, scikit-image, plotly-geo

COMPARE “which one is bigger?”

22 charts

Bar chart

px.bar(df, x='agency', y='spend')
Data shape: One label column + one number, one row per label.
Use when: You have a handful of named things with a number each and you want to see which is biggest and by how much.
Watch out: px.bar does NOT group by. Duplicate x values stack into segments instead of summing. Pre-aggregate first.
drawing on scroll

Horizontal bar (ranked)

px.bar(df.sort_values('spend'), x='spend', y='agency', orientation='h')
Data shape: One label column + one number, and the labels are long words.
Use when: Your category names are words, not codes. Sideways labels are readable; rotated ones are not.
Watch out: Sorting inverts: an ASCENDING sort puts the biggest bar at the TOP of a horizontal chart.
drawing on scroll

Grouped bar

px.bar(df, x='agency', y='spend', color='region', barmode='group')
Data shape: Two label columns + one number, one row per pair.
Use when: Every thing is split the same way and you want to compare the splits side by side rather than as a total.
drawing on scroll

Sorted bar via categoryorder

px.bar(...).update_xaxes(categoryorder='total descending')
Data shape: One label column + one number, in whatever order the query returned.
Use when: You want the biggest first and would rather not sort in SQL or pandas. 18 orderings are built in.
Watch out: Silent no-op unless the axis resolves to type 'category'. Integer codes on x need .astype(str) first.
drawing on scroll

Histogram as GROUP BY

px.histogram(df, x='agency', y='award', histfunc='sum')
Data shape: One category column + one number, un-summarised, many rows per category.
Use when: You want a total or average per group and would rather not write the GROUP BY. histfunc does it for you.
Watch out: histfunc takes count, sum, avg, min, max.
drawing on scroll

Box plot (compare groups)

px.box(df, x='agency', y='award')
Data shape: One category column + one number, many rows per category.
Use when: Comparing averages would lie. You want to see which group runs higher AND which has wild outliers.
drawing on scroll

Heatmap of a pivot table

px.imshow(pivot_df, aspect='auto')
Data shape: An already-shaped grid: rows x columns of numbers (a pivot, or df.corr()).
Use when: You have a number for every combination of two things and you want to see which cells run hot.
Watch out: imshow colours a grid you already made. density_heatmap bins raw rows for you. Different jobs. Index and column names become the tick labels for free.
drawing on scroll

Correlation matrix

px.imshow(df.corr(), text_auto='.2f', zmin=-1, zmax=1)
Data shape: Several number columns describing the same rows.
Use when: You want one number for how strongly every pair moves together, printed in the cell.
Watch out: Use a diverging scale pinned at zero. A sequential scale here hides which correlations are negative.
drawing on scroll

Heatmap (go.Heatmap, long form)

go.Heatmap(x=cols, y=rows, z=grid, xgap=1, ygap=1)
Data shape: Two category columns + one number for every pair.
Use when: Same question as a pivot heatmap, built by hand so you control the gaps, the cell text and the colour bar.
drawing on scroll

Annotated heatmap

ff.create_annotated_heatmap(z=grid, x=cols, y=rows)
Data shape: A small grid of numbers where the exact value matters as much as the colour.
Use when: The reader must read numbers off the grid, not eyeball them against a colour ramp.
drawing on scroll

Contour of a computed grid

go.Contour(z=grid, contours=dict(showlabels=True))
Data shape: A value already computed across a grid of two inputs (a model surface, a cost function).
Use when: You want ridges and valleys, not a cell-by-cell readout. Like elevation rings on a walking map.
Watch out: No px route. px.density_contour bins raw points; go.Contour draws a grid you already have.
drawing on scroll

Constraint contour (feasible region)

go.Contour(z=grid, contours=dict(type='constraint', operation='[]', value=[0, 3]))
Data shape: The same computed grid, but the question is pass/fail rather than how much.
Use when: You want the shaded area where a condition holds - under a cap, inside a tolerance band.
Watch out: operation accepts 13 values including '[]' for 'between these two numbers'.
drawing on scroll

Wind rose (polar bar)

px.bar_polar(df, r='frequency', theta='direction')
Data shape: A wrap-around category (compass point, hour of day, month) + a number.
Use when: Your categories loop back on themselves. On a straight axis December and January sit at opposite ends, which is a lie.
drawing on scroll

Dumbbell chart

2 x go.Scatter + one add_shape line per row
Data shape: One entity column + exactly two numbers (before and after, budget and actual).
Use when: The gap between the two numbers IS the story. The bar's length is the change, read straight off the chart.
Watch out: No go.Dumbbell exists. You build it from two scatters and a line shape per row.
drawing on scroll

Lollipop chart

go.Scatter(mode='markers') + a line shape from zero
Data shape: One label column + one number, many labels.
Use when: Same question as a bar chart, but 30 fat bars is a wall of ink and 30 stalks is not.
drawing on scroll

Cleveland dot plot

two go.Scatter(mode='markers') sharing a category axis
Data shape: One entity column + two or more comparable numbers.
Use when: Several measures per entity, and you want them read against each other without stacking or grouping bars.
drawing on scroll

Marimekko / mosaic

go.Bar(x=centres, y=share, width=array, offset=0)
Data shape: Two category columns + a number, where the categories are wildly different sizes.
Use when: A 100% stacked bar makes a tiny category shout as loud as a huge one. Bar WIDTH fixes that: width = how big the category is.
Watch out: No go.Marimekko. The trick is passing an array to width= and setting offset=0.
drawing on scroll

Two-level category axis

go.Bar(x=[[outer, outer, ...], [inner, inner, ...]])
Data shape: One number nested under two category levels (quarter, then region).
Use when: You want the grouping printed on the axis itself instead of explained in a legend.
Watch out: Set by handing x a list of TWO parallel lists. The axis type becomes 'multicategory'.
drawing on scroll

Small multiples (facets)

px.histogram(df, x='award', facet_col='agency')
Data shape: One number + one or two low-cardinality category columns.
Use when: The question is 'does this hold in EVERY group, or only some?' Colour puts them all on one panel and they turn to mush.
Watch out: Facets share axes by default. update_yaxes(matches=None) unshares them - a deliberate choice, since unshared panels look comparable and are not.
drawing on scroll

Facet grid (figure factory)

ff.create_facet_grid(df, x='inspections', y='violations', facet_col='region')
Data shape: Two numbers + a category.
Use when: You want faceting but you are not building the figure with plotly express.
drawing on scroll

Table

go.Table(header=dict(values=cols), cells=dict(values=[col1, col2]))
Data shape: Rows and columns, where the exact numbers are the receipt.
Use when: A chart of 200 ranked rows is unreadable and a scrollable table is not. Use it beside the chart that summarises it.
Watch out: cells.values is COLUMN-major - a list per column. Feeding it rows silently transposes your table.
drawing on scroll

Table (figure factory)

ff.create_table(df)
Data shape: A small dataframe.
Use when: You want a styled table in one call and do not care to configure fills and formats yourself.

DISTRIBUTE “how is it spread out?”

20 charts

Histogram

px.histogram(df, x='award', nbins=50, marginal='box')
Data shape: One number column, many rows. No categories needed.
Use when: You want to know what is typical, how wide the spread runs, and whether the tail is long. Plotly does the counting.
Watch out: bargap=0 so the bins touch. A gap implies a gap in the data that is not there. marginal adds a box, violin or rug strip on top.
drawing on scroll

Histogram, normalised and cumulative

px.histogram(df, x='award', histnorm='percent', cumulative=True)
Data shape: One number column, many rows, often split by a group.
Use when: The question is 'what share of rows sit below X', or two differently-sized groups need comparing fairly on one axis.
drawing on scroll

ECDF - the share below any value

px.ecdf(df, x='award', color='agency')
Data shape: One number column spread across thousands of entities, especially money.
Use when: You want to read off 'what fraction is below THIS amount' for every possible amount at once, with no bins to argue about.
Watch out: ecdfnorm: probability / percent / None (raw counts). Two overlaid ECDFs are a fair fight; two overlaid histograms are a mess.
drawing on scroll

ECDF, complementary, log-log

px.ecdf(df, x='award', ecdfmode='complementary', log_x=True, log_y=True)
Data shape: One money-like number across thousands of entities.
Use when: The question is concentration: are the top 1% holding half the money? On log-log a power law draws as a STRAIGHT LINE, so a kink is an anomaly you spot with your eye.
Watch out: 'complementary' flips it to 'what share sit at or ABOVE this value' - the survival curve.
drawing on scroll

ECDF weighted by a count column

px.ecdf(df, x='bucket', y='n')
Data shape: One number + a count/weight column - i.e. rows you already aggregated.
Use when: Your warehouse returned one row per unique value with a count beside it. y= weights each row by that count instead of treating it as one.
drawing on scroll

Box plot

px.box(df, x='agency', y='award', notched=True)
Data shape: One number column, optionally split by a category.
Use when: Where is the middle, how wide is the middle half, and who is a straggler. Box = 25th to 75th percentile, line = median.
Watch out: points: 'outliers' (default), 'suspectedoutliers', 'all', False. If two notches do not overlap, the medians differ meaningfully - a significance test you read by eye.
drawing on scroll

Box from pre-computed quartiles

go.Box(q1=..., median=..., q3=..., lowerfence=..., upperfence=...)
Data shape: Five summary numbers per group, computed in SQL. NOT raw rows.
Use when: You have 800 million rows. Run APPROX_PERCENTILE in the warehouse and ship five numbers per group instead of ten million.
Watch out: Same picture, roughly 7 KB instead of 2.7 MB. The single biggest scale lever in the library.
drawing on scroll

Violin

px.violin(df, x='group', y='score', box=True)
Data shape: One number split by a category, where you suspect the shape is lumpy.
Use when: A box plot hides two humps completely. A violin's width at each height is how many rows sit at that value, so two humps show as two bulges.
Watch out: scalemode='count' makes fatness proportional to how many rows are in the group. The default makes a group of 12 shout as loud as a group of 12,000.
drawing on scroll

Split violin (back to back)

go.Violin(side='negative') + go.Violin(side='positive'), violinmode='overlay'
Data shape: One number, one grouping category, and one two-value split (year, region, before/after).
Use when: You want two distributions compared on the exact same axis with no eye travel between panels.
drawing on scroll

Ridgeline

stacked go.Violin(side='positive', orientation='h'), violingap=0
Data shape: One number + one category with 5-40 levels (states, years, agencies).
Use when: 50 states as bars is 50 numbers. 50 states as ridges is 50 DISTRIBUTIONS - fat right tails versus fat middles, which is the difference between one bad actor and a systemic policy.
Watch out: No go.Ridgeline. violingap=0 is the load-bearing trick that fuses the ridges into one landscape. On a log x-axis you must set an explicit range: the smoothed curve runs past zero, and the log of a negative number is undefined, which silently breaks the gridlines.
drawing on scroll

Strip plot - every single row

px.strip(df, x='agency', y='award')
Data shape: One number + one category, with fewer than about 500 rows per category.
Use when: Summarising five points would be a lie, and you want to be able to point at ONE dot and name it.
Watch out: px.strip is secretly a box trace with the box made invisible (boxpoints='all', transparent fill and line).
drawing on scroll

Beeswarm

go.Scatter(x=values, y=small random jitter, mode='markers')
Data shape: One number column, a few hundred rows.
Use when: Same as a strip plot but you control the jitter, so overlapping points spread out instead of stacking into a solid stripe.
drawing on scroll

Raincloud

go.Violin(side='positive') + go.Box + jittered go.Scatter
Data shape: One number column, a few hundred rows.
Use when: You want the shape, the summary and the raw rows all at once, so nobody can accuse the summary of hiding something.
drawing on scroll

2D density heatmap

px.density_heatmap(df, x='inspections', y='violations', nbinsx=40, nbinsy=40)
Data shape: Two number columns with far too many rows to plot as dots.
Use when: The scatter has gone to a solid blob. This bins both axes and colours the cells, so you can see the blob's interior.
Watch out: No color= parameter - the colour channel is already spent on density. Its sibling density_contour does have one.
drawing on scroll

2D density contour

px.density_contour(df, x='inspections', y='violations', color='region')
Data shape: Two number columns plus a group you want to overlay.
Use when: Same binning as the density heatmap, drawn as rings. Better for asking whether two clouds sit in different places.
drawing on scroll

2D density (figure factory)

ff.create_2d_density(x, y)
Data shape: Two number columns, many rows.
Use when: You want the scatter, the contours and both edge histograms assembled for you in one call.
drawing on scroll

Isosurface - the 3D threshold shell

go.Isosurface(x, y, z, value=..., isomin=..., isomax=...)
Data shape: Four equal-length arrays: x, y, z positions and a value at each - a 3D grid.
Use when: A number measured throughout a volume (concentration, temperature, dose) and you want the boundary of the hot zone.
drawing on scroll

Volume - the whole 3D cloud

go.Volume(x, y, z, value=..., opacity=0.12, surface_count=16)
Data shape: The same four arrays as isosurface.
Use when: You want the whole gradient rather than one boundary. Many nested shells at once.
Watch out: Untuned you get fog. opacityscale is what makes the low-value regions see-through.
drawing on scroll

Distplot (histogram + smooth curve + rug)CANNOT RENDER HERE

ff.create_distplot([values], ['label'])
Data shape: One or more number columns.
Use when: You want a histogram with a smoothed curve over it plus a rug - one tick mark per row along the axis, so you see individual rows and the shape together.
Why not here: Needs scipy, which is not installed here. `pip install scipy` unblocks it. px.histogram(marginal='rug') plus px.violin(box=True) covers most of it with no extra package.

Violin with smoothed curve (figure factory)CANNOT RENDER HERE

ff.create_violin(df, data_header='v', group_header='g')
Data shape: One number + one grouping column.
Use when: The figure-factory violin recipe, with the smoothing computed in Python rather than the browser.
Why not here: Needs scipy. go.Violin and px.violin work fine without it - that curve is computed by JavaScript in the browser.

26 charts

Scatter plot

px.scatter(df, x='inspections', y='violations', color='region')
Data shape: Two number columns, one row per thing.
Use when: Do these two move together, and who are the weirdos sitting far from the pack?
Watch out: px.scatter has the most options of any px function (49). It silently switches to WebGL rendering above 1000 points.
drawing on scroll

Scatter with edge distributions

px.scatter(df, x=..., y=..., marginal_x='histogram', marginal_y='violin')
Data shape: Two number columns, one row per thing.
Use when: You want the relationship AND each number's own spread, without building three charts and lining them up.
Watch out: marginal_x / marginal_y exist on exactly 3 functions: scatter, density_contour, density_heatmap.
drawing on scroll

Scatter with a trend line

px.scatter(df, x=..., y=..., trendline='rolling', trendline_options=dict(window=40))
Data shape: Two number columns where one is naturally ordered.
Use when: The cloud has a direction and you want it drawn, not guessed at.
Watch out: trendline='ols' and 'lowess' need statsmodels, which is NOT installed here. rolling / expanding / ewm are pure pandas and work now.
drawing on scroll

Bubble chart

px.scatter(df, x=..., y=..., size='employees', color='fines')
Data shape: Two numbers on the axes plus a third as dot size and a fourth as colour.
Use when: Four variables at once, and the question is which entities are extreme on several of them together.
Watch out: Set marker.sizemode='area' or big values visually lie - a doubled radius is a quadrupled blob.
drawing on scroll

WebGL scatter (huge point counts)

px.scatter(df, x=..., y=..., render_mode='webgl') # or go.Scattergl(...)
Data shape: Two number columns with tens of thousands of rows.
Use when: Same question as a plain scatter, but the page has gone sticky. This draws on the graphics card instead.
Watch out: Fewer styling options than plain scatter (66 props vs 77) and it rasterises on PDF export. Casting to float32 first halves the bytes shipped to the browser - measured 562 KB down to 283 KB for these 25,000 points.
drawing on scroll

Quadrant scatter

px.scatter(...).add_hline(y=median).add_vline(x=median)
Data shape: Two number columns plus a rule about what counts as high.
Use when: You want to name a corner - 'high fines AND low inspections' - rather than describe a slope.
drawing on scroll

Scatter plot matrix (splom)

px.scatter_matrix(df, dimensions=[...])
Data shape: Four to eight number columns describing the same rows, no hypothesis yet.
Use when: Which PAIRS of these are related at all? Every column plotted against every other, in one grid.
Watch out: Ships with dragmode='select' - lasso in one cell and the same rows highlight in every other cell.
drawing on scroll

Scatterplot matrix (figure factory)

ff.create_scatterplotmatrix(df, diag='histogram')
Data shape: Several number columns on the same rows.
Use when: Same question as a splom, assembled from ordinary scatter and histogram traces so you can restyle every panel.
drawing on scroll

Parallel coordinates

px.parallel_coordinates(df, dimensions=[...], color='risk')
Data shape: One row per entity and four to ten NUMBER columns.
Use when: Which entities are high on several measures at once? No scatter answers that past two columns.
Watch out: Drag a bracket on any axis and every line outside it greys out - a live multi-column WHERE clause. Warning: it has no hover tooltips.
drawing on scroll

Parallel coordinates with a locked filter

go.Parcoords(dimensions=[dict(label=..., values=..., constraintrange=[20, 50])])
Data shape: The same shape, but you want the page to open already filtered.
Use when: You are publishing a finding and want the reader to land on the subset that matters, still able to widen it.
drawing on scroll

3D scatter

px.scatter_3d(df, x=..., y=..., z=..., color=...)
Data shape: Three number columns per row.
Use when: Do all three move together, and do the rows split into clumps you cannot see in two dimensions?
Watch out: Honest warning: a 2D scatter with colour and size encodes four columns and is easier to read. Use 3D only when the reader can rotate it.
drawing on scroll

3D line

px.line_3d(df, x=..., y=..., z=...)
Data shape: Three numbers in sequence.
Use when: What path does this trace through three-dimensional space? A trajectory, not a cloud.
drawing on scroll

3D ribbon (filled 3D line)

go.Scatter3d(mode='lines', surfaceaxis=1, surfacecolor='...')
Data shape: Three numbers in sequence, where one dimension is a baseline.
Use when: The 3D equivalent of an area chart: drop a filled wall from the line down to a plane so the depth reads.
Watch out: surfaceaxis takes -1, 0, 1 or 2. It is the only thing separating a 3D line from a 3D ribbon.
drawing on scroll

Surface

go.Surface(z=grid)
Data shape: A value computed over a grid of two inputs.
Use when: You want the shape of the response - where the peak is, how steep the sides run.
Watch out: No px route. contours= projects lines onto the surface or the walls of the box.
drawing on scroll

Mesh3d - a solid from a point cloud

go.Mesh3d(x, y, z, alphahull=5)
Data shape: A 3D point cloud, or explicit vertices plus triangle indices.
Use when: You have points in space and want them skinned into a solid shape rather than left as dots.
Watch out: Three routes in: explicit i/j/k triangles, alphahull to auto-wrap a shell, or delaunayaxis for roughly-flat points.

Trisurf (figure factory)

ff.create_trisurf(x, y, z, simplices=triangles)
Data shape: 3D points plus an explicit list of which three points make each triangle.
Use when: You already computed a triangulation and want it coloured and shaded in one call.

Radar / spider chart

go.Scatterpolar(r=[...], theta=[...], fill='toself')
Data shape: Five to eight comparable measures for one to three entities.
Use when: What is this entity's SILHOUETTE, and is that one a different shape? Two entities with the same total can look completely different.
Watch out: No go.Radar. Repeat the first point at the end to close the loop, or use px.line_polar(line_close=True). polar.gridshape='linear' gives the polygonal grid.

Polar scatter / line

px.line_polar(df, r='frequency', theta='direction', line_close=True)
Data shape: A cyclical category or angle + a number.
Use when: The x axis wraps around - hour of day, month, compass bearing - and you want that wrap drawn honestly.

Polar scatter, WebGL

px.scatter_polar(df, r=..., theta=..., render_mode='webgl')
Data shape: The same polar shape with tens of thousands of points.
Use when: The polar chart has gone sticky. Same trick as scattergl, on a circle.

Two units on one x axis (secondary y)

make_subplots(specs=[[{'secondary_y': True}]])
Data shape: Two numbers on very different scales sharing one x axis.
Use when: A 0-1 rate plotted against a 30,000 count flattens to a dead line on the floor. Give it its own axis.
Watch out: Honest warning: dual axes can manufacture a correlation that is not there, purely by choosing the two ranges.

Smith chart

go.Scattersmith(real=[...], imag=[...])
Data shape: Complex numbers from radio-frequency or transmission-line measurements.
Use when: Electrical impedance. Outside RF engineering this has essentially no use - it is here so nothing is hidden from you.
drawing on scroll

Carpet - the graph paper itself

go.Carpet(a=..., b=..., x=..., y=...)
Data shape: Two independent variables that are not perpendicular - moving A also shifts where B sits.
Use when: Engineering and aerodynamics charts. On its own a carpet draws almost nothing: it is the warped grid other traces sit on.
Watch out: No hover. If you are not doing engineering charts with non-perpendicular variables you will never need this.
drawing on scroll

Scattercarpet - points on a warped grid

go.Carpet(carpet='c1') + go.Scattercarpet(a=..., b=..., carpet='c1')
Data shape: Readings taken at (a, b) positions on a non-perpendicular grid.
Use when: Same as a scatter, but the coordinate system itself is warped, so the dot's position means something the axes cannot show.
Watch out: Requires a go.Carpet trace with a matching carpet id already in the figure.
drawing on scroll

Contourcarpet - contours on a warped grid

go.Carpet(carpet='c1') + go.Contourcarpet(a=..., b=..., z=..., carpet='c1')
Data shape: A value measured across a non-perpendicular grid.
Use when: The contour version of the above. Also has no hover.

Ordinary-least-squares / lowess trend lineCANNOT RENDER HERE

px.scatter(df, x=..., y=..., trendline='ols')
Data shape: Two number columns.
Use when: The straight-line fit everybody reaches for, plus the R-squared you get from px.get_trendline_results(fig).
Why not here: Needs statsmodels, which is NOT installed here. Both 'ols' and 'lowess' raise ModuleNotFoundError. `pip install statsmodels` unblocks them. trendline='rolling' / 'expanding' / 'ewm' work today - see the chart above.

Dendrogram (clustering tree)CANNOT RENDER HERE

ff.create_dendrogram(matrix)
Data shape: A matrix of rows to be clustered.
Use when: You want to see which rows group together and at what distance they merge - the tree above a clustered heatmap.
Why not here: Needs scipy. `pip install scipy` unblocks it. A treemap or icicle covers a hierarchy you already know; the dendrogram is for one you want DISCOVERED.

COMPOSE “what is it made of?”

16 charts

Pie / donut

px.pie(df, names='agency', values='spend', hole=0.45)
Data shape: One category column + one number that genuinely sums to a real whole, under about six slices.
Use when: Roughly what share is each? Past six slices nobody can read it - use a sorted bar instead.
Watch out: The only part-of-whole chart in px that facets. hole= makes it a donut, which at least puts a number in the middle.
drawing on scroll

Stacked bar

px.bar(df, x='agency', y='spend', color='region')
Data shape: One category column + a subcategory + a number.
Use when: You want the total AND what is inside each total, for several things at once.
drawing on scroll

100% stacked bar

px.bar(...).update_layout(barnorm='percent')
Data shape: The same shape, when the totals differ wildly.
Use when: The question is whether the MIX differs, not the size. Every bar becomes the same height and shows share.
Watch out: This throws the total away. Only do it when the total genuinely does not matter to the question.
drawing on scroll

Area chart

px.area(df, x='date', y='claims', color='region')
Data shape: A date column + a category + a number.
Use when: How did the total change, and how did the mix inside it change, at the same time?
Watch out: px.area is px.line plus two properties: stackgroup=1 and mode='lines'. That is the entire difference.
drawing on scroll

100% stacked area

px.area(df, ..., groupnorm='fraction')
Data shape: A date column + a category + a number.
Use when: Is one player's SHARE growing? This strips out total growth so composition is the only signal left.
drawing on scroll

Streamgraph

go.Scatter(stackgroup='one', mode='none') per series
Data shape: A date column + several categories + a number.
Use when: Many categories over time where the rise and fall of each band is the story, not exact values.
Watch out: Same stacking as an area chart, drawn centred rather than sitting on a baseline.
drawing on scroll

Treemap

px.treemap(df, path=['agency', 'program', 'vendor'], values='amount')
Data shape: Nested category columns (broad to narrow) + a number.
Use when: Where inside a structure is the mass? Nested rectangles sized by value. Best of the three when comparing SIZES.
Watch out: branchvalues: px sets 'total' for you when you use path=. Building go.Treemap by hand, the default is 'remainder' - and if your SQL already returns parent totals that double-counts silently.
drawing on scroll

Sunburst

px.sunburst(df, path=[...], values='amount')
Data shape: The same nested columns + a number.
Use when: Same question as a treemap, when the DEPTH of the nesting is the story. Concentric rings out from the centre.
Watch out: textinfo='label+percent parent' prints what share each slice is of its own parent - how you find 'one vendor is 80% of one programme'.
drawing on scroll

Icicle

px.icicle(df, path=[...], values='amount')
Data shape: The same nested columns + a number.
Use when: Same question again, when the labels are long words that need horizontal room, or the tree is deep and narrow.
drawing on scroll

Flame graph

go.Icicle(tiling=dict(orientation='v', flip='y'))
Data shape: The same hierarchy, when you want the root at the BOTTOM.
Use when: The profiler's view - root at the bottom, children stacking upward. This orientation is the actual reason to pick icicle over treemap.
Watch out: tiling.orientation takes 'v' or 'h'; tiling.flip takes 'x' and/or 'y'.
drawing on scroll

Funnel area

px.funnel_area(names=stages, values=counts)
Data shape: Ordered stages + shrinking counts.
Use when: Same data as a funnel, drawn as a cone in its own box so it sits next to pies rather than on axes.
drawing on scroll

Ternary scatter

px.scatter_ternary(df, a='federal', b='state', c='private')
Data shape: Three numbers per row that are parts of one whole.
Use when: Who is balanced, who is lopsided, and do the lopsided ones cluster? The ONLY chart that shows three-way composition for many entities at once.
Watch out: Dead centre means one third each. A stacked bar can only show a handful of entities; this shows hundreds.
drawing on scroll

Ternary line

px.line_ternary(df, a=..., b=..., c=...)
Data shape: The same three-part mix, in sequence.
Use when: How did the three-way split DRIFT over time - did it move toward one corner?
drawing on scroll

Waffle / unit chart

go.Heatmap(z=100_cell_grid, xgap=3, ygap=3)
Data shape: One category column + a share of 100.
Use when: Percentages that a reader should be able to COUNT. One square is one percent, so 37% is 37 countable squares.
drawing on scroll

Population pyramid

two go.Bar(orientation='h'), one side negated, barmode='relative'
Data shape: An ordered band column (age group) + two counts.
Use when: Two populations compared band by band, mirrored around a shared spine.
drawing on scroll

Ternary contourCANNOT RENDER HERE

ff.create_ternary_contour(coords, values)
Data shape: Three parts summing to a whole, plus a fourth measured value.
Use when: Contour bands drawn INSIDE the triangle - 'what is the yield at each blend?'
Why not here: Needs scikit-image, which is not installed here. `pip install scikit-image` unblocks it. px.scatter_ternary with color= shows the same fourth variable as dot colour, with no extra package.

FLOW “what moves where?”

9 charts

Sankey diagram

go.Sankey(node=dict(label=names), link=dict(source=idx, target=idx, value=amounts))
Data shape: A from-column, a to-column and an amount - any GROUP BY a, b, SUM(x) you have ever run.
Use when: Where did the money actually come from and where did it end up? Two bar charts cannot tell you WHICH source fed WHICH destination, and that relationship is the story.
Watch out: The trap: link.source and link.target must be INTEGER POSITIONS into node.label, not the names. Strings validate cleanly and then render nothing.
drawing on scroll

Sankey with grouped nodes and arrow links

go.Sankey(node=dict(groups=[[3, 4]], align='left'), link=dict(arrowlen=15))
Data shape: The same edge list, when some nodes should be collapsed into one box.
Use when: Several destinations are really one thing, or you want the ribbons to read directionally with arrow tips.
Watch out: node.groups merges nodes; node.align takes justify / left / right / centre; link.arrowlen puts a point on each ribbon.
drawing on scroll

Parallel categories

px.parallel_categories(df, dimensions=['agency', 'region', 'band'])
Data shape: Three to six CATEGORY columns describing the same rows.
Use when: Which combinations actually occur together, and which never do? Ribbon thickness is how many rows took that path.
Watch out: Needs zero reshaping - hand it the wide table. It silently drops any column with more than 50 distinct values. Feed it a pre-aggregated counts= array to scale.
drawing on scroll

Funnel

px.funnel(df, x='cases', y='stage')
Data shape: Ordered stages + a count that shrinks at each one.
Use when: Where does the process leak? A bar chart of stage counts makes you do the subtraction in your head, and the story is the biggest GAP, not the biggest bar.
Watch out: textinfo='percent previous' prints the drop-off from the step before, straight on the chart.
drawing on scroll

Grouped funnel

px.funnel(df, x='cases', y='stage', color='agency')
Data shape: Ordered stages + a count, for two or more entities.
Use when: Two agencies run the same process and you want to see who leaks where.
drawing on scroll

Cone - a 3D vector field

go.Cone(x, y, z, u, v, w)
Data shape: Six equal-length arrays: three for position, three for direction.
Use when: Each point in space has a direction and a strength - wind, current, magnetic field - and you want to see which way it pushes.
drawing on scroll

Streamtube - the paths through a field

go.Streamtube(x, y, z, u, v, w)
Data shape: The same six arrays as cone.
Use when: The question is about PATHS, not arrows: where does something released here end up?
drawing on scroll

Quiver plot (2D arrows)

ff.create_quiver(x, y, u, v)
Data shape: Four arrays: two for position, two for direction, all in 2D.
Use when: The flat version of a cone plot. Each arrow shows direction and strength at that spot.
drawing on scroll

Streamlines (2D)

ff.create_streamline(x, y, u, v)
Data shape: A 2D grid of positions plus a direction at each.
Use when: Same field as the quiver, drawn as continuous paths rather than separate arrows.
drawing on scroll

RANK “who is on top, and did it change?”

6 charts

Ranked horizontal bar

px.bar(df.sort_values('score'), x='score', y='entity', orientation='h')
Data shape: One entity column + one number.
Use when: Who is on top right now. The default and usually the correct answer.
Watch out: Sort ASCENDING for a horizontal bar - plotly draws bottom-to-top, so ascending puts the winner at the top.
drawing on scroll

Bump chart

px.line(df, x='year', y='rank').update_yaxes(autorange='reversed')
Data shape: One entity column + a number + a date, over many periods.
Use when: Who is climbing and who is falling? A grouped bar of 5 entities x 10 years is 50 bars your eye cannot follow. Here CROSSINGS are visible events.
Watch out: No px.bump. The whole trick is autorange='reversed' so rank 1 sits at the top.
drawing on scroll

Slope chart

px.line(df[df.year.isin([first, last])], x='year', y='score', color='entity')
Data shape: One entity column + one number at exactly two points in time.
Use when: Then versus now. Up-sloping and down-sloping separate instantly, and the steepest line is the biggest mover.
Watch out: A before/after grouped bar makes the reader compute the change. The slope IS the change.
drawing on scroll

Pareto chart

make_subplots(secondary_y=True) + sorted go.Bar + cumulative % go.Scatter
Data shape: One entity column + one number, many entities.
Use when: How few entities account for most of the total? Read across at 80% on the right axis to find the answer.
drawing on scroll

Rank as a heatmap

go.Heatmap(z=rank_matrix, x=years, y=entities)
Data shape: One entity column x one period column + a rank or a value.
Use when: The whole leaderboard's history in one grid. 50 numbers as bars is unreadable; as a grid it is a picture.
drawing on scroll

Legend as an isolate control

fig.update_layout(legend=dict(itemclick='toggleothers'))
Data shape: Many series on one chart.
Use when: Twenty lines and the reader wants one. One click isolates it instead of nineteen clicks to hide the rest.
Watch out: itemclick: 'toggle' / 'toggleothers' / False. Pair with visible='legendonly' to start with only the top few showing.
drawing on scroll

LOCATE “where?”

17 charts

Choropleth (built-in outlines)

px.choropleth(df, locations='state', locationmode='USA-states', color='rate', scope='usa')
Data shape: One place-code column (state code, ISO country code) + one number.
Use when: Which places run high. Start here: the built-in outlines mean you need NO geojson file at all.
Watch out: locationmode takes 'ISO-3', 'USA-states', 'country names'. The outline map needs no tiles and no token, and unlike tile maps it can be faceted.
drawing on scroll

Diverging choropleth

px.choropleth(..., color_continuous_scale='RdBu', color_continuous_midpoint=0)
Data shape: One place code + one number that can sit above OR below a baseline.
Use when: The number is a change or a rate, so the reader needs to see instantly which side of zero each place is on.
Watch out: Without the midpoint, the neutral colour lands wherever the data average happens to be, and 'white means zero' silently becomes a lie.
drawing on scroll

Small-multiple maps (facets)

px.choropleth(df, ..., facet_col='year')
Data shape: A place code + a number + one more low-cardinality column.
Use when: One map per year, side by side, on a shared colour scale.
Watch out: Only the outline (_geo) family facets. The tile-map family (scatter_map, density_map, choropleth_map) cannot.
drawing on scroll

Geo scatter (bubble map)

px.scatter_geo(df, lat='lat', lon='lon', size='amount')
Data shape: A latitude column + a longitude column (+ a number for size).
Use when: Where are these, and are they clustered? Circles sized by value beat a choropleth for raw COUNTS, because a choropleth of counts is a population map wearing a costume.
drawing on scroll

Geo connection map

px.line_geo(df, lat=..., lon=..., color='route')
Data shape: Origin and destination coordinate pairs.
Use when: What connects to what, geographically - shipments, ownership chains, transfers.
drawing on scroll

Orthographic globe

px.scatter_geo(..., projection='orthographic')
Data shape: Any lat/lon or place-code data.
Use when: The default flat projection distorts area badly at the poles. 22 projections are built in; this one is a globe.
Watch out: projection takes 22 values. scope takes world / usa / europe / asia / africa / north america / south america. fitbounds auto-zooms to your data.
drawing on scroll

Tile-map scatter

px.scatter_map(df, lat='lat', lon='lon', size='amount')
Data shape: A latitude column + a longitude column.
Use when: Same as a geo scatter, but the reader needs to zoom in and see the actual streets under the dots.
Watch out: Built with map_style='white-bg' so this page needs no tile server. Switch to 'carto-darkmatter' or 'open-street-map' when you have internet.
drawing on scroll

Tile-map density (hotspot blur)

px.density_map(df, lat=..., lon=..., z='amount', radius=25)
Data shape: So many lat/lon points that individual dots turn to mush.
Use when: Where is the hotspot? radius= controls the blur size in pixels and is the only knob that really matters.
drawing on scroll

Tile-map choropleth (your own boundaries)

px.choropleth_map(df, geojson=gj, locations='zone', featureidkey='properties.zone', color='rate')
Data shape: One row per named region + one number, plus a geojson of the boundaries.
Use when: The regions are not countries or states - census tracts, ZIPs, precincts, sales territories - and the question is which neighbourhoods are high.
Watch out: featureidkey names the property INSIDE your geojson that your locations column matches. Default is 'id'.
drawing on scroll

Line map (tile)

px.line_map(df, lat=..., lon=..., color='route')
Data shape: Sequences of lat/lon points that form a journey.
Use when: Routes on a zoomable tile map rather than a fixed outline.
drawing on scroll

Hexbin map

ff.create_hexbin_map(lat=..., lon=..., nx_hexagon=20)
Data shape: Thousands of lat/lon points and no natural boundary to aggregate into.
Use when: Bins the points into equal-size hexagons, which kills the 'big states look important' distortion completely.
Watch out: There is no hexbin TRACE. This factory builds hexagons out of a choroplethmap.
drawing on scroll

Geo subplot grid

make_subplots(rows=1, cols=3, specs=[[{'type': 'geo'}] * 3])
Data shape: Several maps that need to sit in one figure.
Use when: One map per measure or per period, hand-built rather than faceted, so each panel can be a different map entirely.
Watch out: specs type 'geo' is a real cell type. It is missing from most cheat sheets, which only list xy / scene / polar / ternary / map / domain.
drawing on scroll

Image as a plot layer

go.Image(z=rgb_array)
Data shape: Actual pixels: a scan, a floor plan, a screenshot, a satellite tile.
Use when: The 'map' is a picture, and you want chart marks sitting on top of it in the picture's own coordinates.
Watch out: Also reachable via px.imshow on an H x W x 3 array. Feeding a 2D array instead gives you a heatmap.
drawing on scroll

Deprecated mapbox family

px.scatter_mapbox / line_mapbox / density_mapbox / choropleth_mapbox
Data shape: Exactly the same shapes as the map family above.
Use when: Never, in new code. This is here so you recognise it in old code and know what to replace it with.
Watch out: All four raise a DeprecationWarning on construction. Replace with scatter_map / line_map / density_map / choropleth_map. The only signature difference is mapbox_style= instead of map_style=.
drawing on scroll

Deprecated mapbox: density, choropleth and line

px.density_mapbox(...) / px.choropleth_mapbox(...) / px.line_mapbox(...)
Data shape: Same shapes as density_map, choropleth_map and line_map.
Use when: Legacy maintenance only. Prop-for-prop identical to their replacements.
Watch out: All three deprecated trace types shown together rather than silently dropped. Each px call emits TWO DeprecationWarnings - one from px, one from the underlying go object.
drawing on scroll

Hexbin map (deprecated mapbox twin)

ff.create_hexbin_mapbox(lat=..., lon=..., nx_hexagon=18)
Data shape: The same thousands of lat/lon points.
Use when: Legacy code only. Identical output to create_hexbin_map.
Watch out: On plotly 6.9 this factory already emits the modern choroplethmap trace, so the only thing still 'mapbox' about it is the function name.
drawing on scroll

US county choropleth by FIPSCANNOT RENDER HERE

ff.create_choropleth(fips=['06001', ...], values=[...])
Data shape: A FIPS county-code column + a number.
Use when: County-level maps of the whole US, with state outlines drawn on top, in one call.
Why not here: Needs the plotly-geo package, which is not installed here. `pip install plotly-geo` unblocks it. Workaround with no extra package: px.choropleth with a county geojson passed to geojson= and featureidkey='id'.

CHANGE “what happened over time?”

18 charts

Line chart

px.line(df, x='date', y='claims', color='region')
Data shape: One ordered column (usually a date) + one number, optionally per entity.
Use when: Is this going up or down? The single most-used shape in the whole library.
Watch out: px.line connects rows in DATAFRAME ORDER, not sorted order. Unsorted input gives you spaghetti - sort first. And dates arriving as strings sort alphabetically.
drawing on scroll

Step line

px.line(df, x='date', y='rate', line_shape='hv')
Data shape: A date column + a number that HOLDS then JUMPS.
Use when: Regulations, rate schedules, headcounts, price bands. A straight sloping line implies gradual change that never happened.
Watch out: line_shape takes linear / spline / hv / vh / hvh / vhv. 'hv' is the step; 'spline' is a smooth curve.
drawing on scroll

Line with a confidence band

go.Scatter(x=x+x[::-1], y=hi+lo[::-1], fill='toself') then the mean line on top
Data shape: A date column + a central number + an upper and lower bound.
Use when: The estimate has uncertainty and hiding it would be dishonest. The band is the uncertainty, drawn.
Watch out: The trick is one closed polygon: x forwards then backwards, y upper then lower reversed, with fill='toself'.
drawing on scroll

Event markers on a time series

fig.add_vrect(x0=..., x1=..., annotation_text='...') and fig.add_vline(...)
Data shape: Any time series, plus dates when something happened.
Use when: Context that is invisible in the data itself - a rule change, an outage, a lockdown. This is how a chart makes a causal claim visible.
Watch out: layer='below' puts the shading behind the data. Four helpers: add_hline, add_vline, add_hrect, add_vrect.
drawing on scroll

Range slider + range selector

fig.update_xaxes(rangeslider_visible=True, rangeselector=dict(buttons=[...]))
Data shape: A long time series - more than a few hundred points.
Use when: 3,650 daily points crammed into 900 pixels. The mini overview strip and the 1m/6m/YTD buttons let the reader look without you deciding for them.
Watch out: rangeslider and rangeselector exist on xaxis and NOT on yaxis. That asymmetry is most of the size difference between the two axis objects.
drawing on scroll

Rangebreaks - delete the dead time

fig.update_xaxes(rangebreaks=[dict(bounds=['sat', 'mon'])])
Data shape: A time series with structural gaps - weekends, holidays, overnight.
Use when: A price chart with a flat step every weekend is drawing time that does not exist. This removes it from the axis entirely.
drawing on scroll

Zoom-aware date labels

fig.update_xaxes(tickformatstops=[dict(dtickrange=[None, 86400000], value='%H:%M'), ...])
Data shape: A long time series the reader will zoom into.
Use when: Zoomed out you want 'Jan 2024'; zoomed into one day you want '14:30'. Stops swap the format automatically by zoom level.
Watch out: dtickrange is in MILLISECONDS. 86400000 is one day, 604800000 is one week.
drawing on scroll

Bars over periods

px.bar(df, x='month', y='claims')
Data shape: A chunky period column (month, quarter) + a number.
Use when: The periods are countable, not continuous. A line implies you could read a value halfway between two months, and you cannot.
drawing on scroll

Gantt / timeline

px.timeline(df, x_start='start', x_end='end', y='contract')
Data shape: One row per event with a BEGIN date and an END date.
Use when: Who overlapped with whom, and what ran long? Contracts, licences, debarments, employment spells, suspensions.
Watch out: Three arguments are non-negotiable: x_start, x_end and y. Underneath it is a bar trace with the start dates in base= and the durations in milliseconds in x=.
drawing on scroll

Gantt (figure factory)

ff.create_gantt(list_of_dicts)
Data shape: Task, Start and Finish per row.
Use when: The same shape, with the older factory that colours by a named column and adds a date axis for you.
drawing on scroll

Waterfall

go.Waterfall(measure=[...], x=labels, y=deltas)
Data shape: A starting total, a list of signed changes, and an ending total.
Use when: The number went from 100 to 110 - what were the PIECES? Two bars say 'it went up 10'. This says '40 arrived and 30 left', which is a completely different story.
Watch out: measure tags each bar 'absolute', 'relative' or 'total'. Without it you just get a bar chart. The validator does not check the strings, so a typo silently renders as a relative step.
drawing on scroll

Candlestick

go.Candlestick(x=dates, open=..., high=..., low=..., close=...)
Data shape: One date column + four price-like numbers per period.
Use when: Did it close above or below where it opened, and how wild was the swing inside the period?
Watch out: Plotly auto-adds a rangeslider under candlesticks. Kill it with xaxis_rangeslider_visible=False.
drawing on scroll

OHLC bars

go.Ohlc(x=dates, open=..., high=..., low=..., close=...)
Data shape: The same four price columns per period.
Use when: Same question as a candlestick. This is the low-ink version, which reads better when you cram hundreds of periods into one width.
drawing on scroll

Candlestick (figure factory)

ff.create_candlestick(open, high, low, close, dates)
Data shape: The same four price columns.
Use when: The factory recipe - it builds the same picture out of ordinary box traces you can restyle.

OHLC (figure factory)

ff.create_ohlc(open, high, low, close, dates)
Data shape: The same four price columns.
Use when: The factory version of the OHLC bar, built from scatter traces.
drawing on scroll

Calendar heatmap

go.Heatmap(z=weekday_by_week_grid, xgap=2, ygap=2)
Data shape: A date column + a count.
Use when: Is there a weekly or seasonal rhythm? Filings clustering on the last day of a quarter show up as a stripe you cannot see in a line chart.
Watch out: No calendar-heatmap chart type exists. You reshape to a 7 x 52 grid yourself.
drawing on scroll

Entity x period heatmap

go.Heatmap(z=matrix, zmid=0, colorscale='RdBu')
Data shape: One entity column x one period column + a number that straddles zero.
Use when: 50 entities over 10 years is 500 numbers. As bars it is unreadable; as a grid you spot the unusual cells at a glance.
drawing on scroll

Animation over time

px.scatter(df, ..., animation_frame='year', animation_group='entity', range_x=[...], range_y=[...])
Data shape: Two numbers + an entity + a time column.
Use when: How did the whole picture move, year by year? A grid of 10 years is 10 things to compare from memory; motion makes the change itself the thing you see.
Watch out: Two non-negotiable rules: set range_x/range_y by hand or the axes rescale each frame and everything appears to stand still, and set animation_group so a dot glides instead of teleporting.

CONNECT “what links to what?”

4 charts

Node-link network

one go.Scatter(mode='lines') with None between each pair, plus a go.Scatter for the nodes
Data shape: An edge list plus x/y positions you computed yourself.
Use when: Who connects to whom, as a web rather than a tree. Plotly has NO network trace - this is the standard hand-built recipe.
Watch out: The None between each pair breaks the line, so all 400 edges live in ONE trace instead of 400. That is the difference between a chart that renders and a page that hangs.
drawing on scroll

Arc diagram

go.Scatter(mode='lines') with a semicircle of points per edge, nodes on one axis
Data shape: An edge list where the nodes have a natural ORDER.
Use when: Same links as a network, but the nodes stay in your chosen order (time, size, alphabet) so you can see whether links are mostly local or mostly long-range.
Watch out: Not a chart type. Each arc is a half-circle of points appended to one scatter trace, separated by None.
drawing on scroll

Overlap matrix

px.imshow(overlap_matrix, text_auto=True)
Data shape: A square grid of how much every thing shares with every other thing.
Use when: Which two datasets can I actually join? A network diagram of 1,000 nodes is a hairball; a sorted 1,000 x 1,000 grid is readable and zoomable.
Watch out: For 'entity appears in 2 of 5 datasets' there is no Venn or UpSet chart in plotly - build a bar chart of set-combination counts instead.
drawing on scroll

Set-combination bar (UpSet's top half)

px.bar on a table of combination -> count
Data shape: One row per entity + a boolean column per set it belongs to.
Use when: Which COMBINATIONS of memberships are common? This is the honest substitute for a Venn diagram past three sets.
Watch out: Plotly has no Venn and no UpSet chart. Count the combinations in pandas and plot them as a sorted bar.

SINGLE VALUE “one number that matters”

7 charts

Indicator - number and delta

go.Indicator(mode='number+delta', value=..., delta=dict(reference=...))
Data shape: One number, plus a prior value to compare it against.
Use when: What is it right now, and is it up or down? This is the KPI tile. There is NO px.indicator.
Watch out: The smallest trace in the library (24 properties). No hover, no legend. It is a domain trace, so in a subplot grid the cell needs type='indicator' or 'domain'.

Indicator - gauge dial

go.Indicator(mode='gauge+number', gauge=dict(shape='angular', steps=[...], threshold=...))
Data shape: One number, a scale it lives on, and a target.
Use when: Where does this sit between bad and good, and are we past the line? steps colour the bands, threshold draws the target.

Indicator - bullet bar

go.Indicator(mode='number+gauge+delta', gauge=dict(shape='bullet'))
Data shape: One number, a target, and good/ok/bad bands.
Use when: The compact version of the dial. Several of these stack into a scoreboard where a round gauge would not fit.

KPI row

make_subplots(rows=1, cols=4, specs=[[{'type': 'indicator'}] * 4])
Data shape: Four numbers, each with a prior value.
Use when: The header strip of a dashboard, as one figure rather than four.
Watch out: Indicator is a DOMAIN trace. In a subplot grid the cell must be declared type='indicator' (or 'domain') or the trace silently refuses to land.

Bullet chart (figure factory)

ff.create_bullet(df, markers='point', measures='performance', ranges='range')
Data shape: One label + a value + a target + qualitative bands.
Use when: The pre-built target-versus-actual bar, if you would rather not wire gauge.shape='bullet' yourself.

Number with a sparkline behind it

go.Indicator(domain=...) + go.Scatter(fill='tozeroy') with both axes hidden
Data shape: One number plus the short series that produced it.

go.Table with a single highlighted row

What this page needs from the network. This build loads plotly.js from cdn.plot.ly, so the whole page needs internet to draw anything. Rebuild with --offline to inline the library (~5 MB file) and remove that dependency. Separately, the outline maps (choropleth, scatter_geo) fetch their country shapes from cdn.plot.ly when the page opens, so those specific panels need internet even in --offline mode. Every other chart is self-contained once the library loads.

What this page cannot show you. Static image export needs kaleido, which is not installed — interactive HTML works, PNG and SVG from Python do not.

Rebuild with python bench/wall.py.
